intro: This unit visits two rooms. The first is the roda, the circle where capoeira is played in Brazil. The second is the boxing ring, a roped square that grew out of English prize fights. Both have music, rules or ceremonies that tell people when to begin and when to stop.

Both arts faced the law. Brazil's Penal Code of 1890 made capoeira a crime, two years after slavery ended. In England and America, bare-knuckle prize fights were often illegal until written rules, gloves and state commissions changed the sport. Schools, gyms, churches and governments each made choices about these arts.

By the end, you will be able to name the people who opened schools and wrote rules, such as Mestre Bimba, Mestre Pastinha and John Graham Chambers. You will read dates in order, from 1743 to 2014. You will explain how a gym, a school association and a heritage office each shape a martial art.
bigQuestion: How do laws, schools and rulebooks decide where a martial art is allowed to happen?

title: Circle and Ring

chapters.title: A Bow, a Song, a Circle
chapters.bigQuestion: How did capoeira go from a crime in Brazil's law books to a treasure the world protects?

story.title: The Wall in Salvador
story.kicker: In a capoeira school in Bahia, the wall tells a story of change.
paragraphs: Salvador is an old port city in Bahia, a state in northeast Brazil. Its hilly old center is called the Pelourinho. On a narrow street there, a capoeira school opens its door in the afternoon. Students hang their bags on hooks by the stairs.

On one wall hang three berimbaus. Each is a long wooden bow with one wire and a round gourd. Next to them hangs a framed page. It is a copy of Brazil's Penal Code of 1890. One article on that page made capoeira a crime.

Beside the old law hangs a newer frame. It shows the year 2014. That year, UNESCO, a United Nations group that protects culture, named the capoeira circle a treasure for all people. The two frames sit side by side, 124 years apart.

A teacher takes down a berimbau. Students set out a drum and two tambourines. People sit in a ring on the floor. The songs will be in Portuguese, the language of Brazil. The same circle that police once broke up is now honored by the world.

The teacher points to the two frames before the music starts. She tells the students that people kept this art alive when the law said no. Many of those people were Black Brazilians whose families had been enslaved. Their names are sung in the songs today.
story.think: Why might a school hang an old law that once banned its own art?

lessons.title: Across the Atlantic
lessons.mainIdea: Capoeira grew in Brazil among enslaved Africans and their children, who were brought there by the Atlantic slave trade.
reading: From the 1500s to the 1800s, Portugal ruled Brazil as a colony. Portuguese owners forced millions of Africans to work there. Enslaved people cut sugarcane, dug for gold and worked in city homes. Historians estimate Brazil received close to five million enslaved Africans. That is more than any other country in the Americas.

Many captives came from Central Africa, from lands that are now Angola and the Congo. Others came from West Africa. They brought languages, music, faiths and games. In Brazil, these traditions mixed together. *Capoeira* grew out of that mix. It joined music, song and movement in a game played by two people.

Historians still debate exactly where capoeira began. Some point to Central African traditions. Others say capoeira was born in Brazil itself. Most agree it grew among Africans and Afro-Brazilians, meaning Brazilians with African ancestors. So capoeira is called an *Afro-Brazilian* art.

words.d: an Afro-Brazilian art that joins music, song and a game played by two people in a circle
about Brazilians with African ancestors and the culture they built
a land ruled by a faraway country

look.title: Two Ideas About Roots
look.text: Historian A says: capoeira keeps pieces of older Central African games and music. Historian B says: capoeira was created in Brazil, by Africans from many places who met there. Both historians agree the people who made it were enslaved Africans and their children.
look.prompt: What do both historians agree on? Where do they disagree?

check.q: Which country ruled Brazil as a colony?
check.why: Portugal ruled Brazil as a colony from the 1500s until 1822.

check.q: What does Afro-Brazilian mean?
choices: about Africans who never left Africa
check.why: Afro-Brazilian describes Brazilians with African ancestors and the culture they built.

check.q: What do historians still debate about capoeira?

check.why: Historians debate how much capoeira came from Central Africa and how much began in Brazil.

lessons.title: A Picture from 1835
lessons.mainIdea: A print by the artist Johann Moritz Rugendas, published around 1835, is one of the oldest pictures of capoeira.
reading: Johann Moritz Rugendas was a German artist. He traveled in Brazil in the 1820s. He drew cities, farms and the people he saw. Back in Europe, his drawings became prints in a book. The book was called *Voyage pittoresque dans le Brésil*, French for a picture trip through Brazil.

One print is titled Jogar Capoëra, or danse de la guerre. The first part is Portuguese for playing capoeira. The French part means war dance. It shows Black Brazilians in a group outdoors. A man plays a drum. Two people face each other in the middle. Others stand around and watch.

The print is a *primary source*, something made at the time being studied. It tells us capoeira was played in public in the early 1800s. It also shows music was there from the start. But Rugendas was an outsider. His French title calls it a war dance. The players themselves called it a game.

words.d: a picture, paper or object made at the time being studied
a picture copied many times from a carved plate or stone

look.title: Reading the Print
look.text: Picture the print. A group of Black Brazilians gathers outdoors. A drummer keeps a beat with his hands. Two people are in the open space in the middle. The rest watch closely. Below the picture, a French caption calls it a war dance. The artist was a visitor from Europe.
look.prompt: What does this picture tell you about capoeira in the 1820s? What might a visitor miss?

check.why: The German artist Rugendas drew the scene in Brazil; the print was published around 1835.

check.q: What is a primary source?
choices: something made at the time being studied
the first chapter of a book
check.why: A primary source was made at the time, like the Rugendas print of the early 1800s.

choices: The artist was an outsider using his own words.

lessons.title: Roda, Jogo and Bateria
lessons.mainIdea: Capoeira happens in a roda, a circle of people, with music from a bateria, a group of instruments.
reading: Capoeira is played in a *roda*. Roda is the Portuguese word for circle or wheel. People stand or sit in a ring. The ring marks the space for the game. Two players enter the middle at a time. When they leave, two others can take a turn.

What happens in the middle is called the *jogo*, Portuguese for game. People say they play capoeira, not fight it. A roda can last a long time. Many people get turns. Everyone in the circle helps by clapping and singing.

The music comes from the *bateria*, the group of instruments. Berimbaus lead it. The atabaque is a tall drum. The pandeiro is a tambourine. The agogô is a double bell. The reco-reco is a notched scraper. In many schools, the lead berimbau player starts and ends the roda.

words.d: Portuguese for circle; the ring of people where capoeira is played
Portuguese for game; the name for what two capoeira players do in the roda
the group of instruments that plays for a capoeira roda

lessons.title: Police Books in Rio
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, police in Rio de Janeiro arrested many people for capoeira and wrote their names in record books.
reading: In 1808, the Portuguese royal family moved to Rio de Janeiro. They were escaping Napoleon's army in Europe. Rio became the capital of the whole Portuguese empire. A year later, in 1809, the city formed a new police guard.

The police kept arrest records. Many entries list people held for capoeira. Most were enslaved men. Others were free Black and mixed-race workers. Punishments were harsh, including whipping. Historians today study these records to learn who played capoeira and where.

Later in the 1800s, groups called *maltas* formed in Rio. A malta was a band of capoeira players tied to one part of the city. Two famous ones were the Nagoas and the Guaiamuns. Politicians sometimes paid maltas to scare voters. That made city leaders even more set against capoeira.

words.d: groups of capoeira players in 1800s Rio de Janeiro, each tied to part of the city
a police list of people held, with names, dates and reasons

look.title: A Line in a Record Book
look.text: Imagine one line in an old police book from Rio. It gives a date, a man's first name, the name of the person who enslaved him, and one word: capoeira. It gives no age, no song and nothing he said.
look.prompt: What can a historian learn from this line? What is missing?

check.why: Maltas were bands of capoeira players, such as the Nagoas and Guaiamuns, each tied to part of Rio.

lessons.title: Freedom, Then a Ban
lessons.mainIdea: Brazil ended slavery in 1888, and just two years later its new Penal Code made capoeira a crime.
reading: On May 13, 1888, Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law, or *Lei Áurea*. It ended slavery in Brazil. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end it. About a year and a half later, in 1889, Brazil's emperor lost power. Brazil became a republic, a country led by elected leaders instead of a king or emperor.

The new republic wrote a new *penal code*, a book of crimes and punishments. It came out in October 1890. Article 402 named capoeira. It said doing capoeira in streets and public squares was a crime. The punishment was two to six months in prison.

The law came right after freedom. Most people who played capoeira were Black Brazilians. Many had just been freed. Historians see the ban as one of several ways leaders tried to control Black Brazilians after 1888. Laws against the Afro-Brazilian faith Candomblé were enforced in these years too.

words.d: the Golden Law of May 13, 1888, which ended slavery in Brazil
a country's book of crimes and their punishments
a country led by elected leaders, not a king or emperor

look.title: Article 402
look.text: Doing, in streets and public squares, the exercises of agility and bodily skill known as capoeiragem ... Penalty: prison for two to six months.
look.cite: Penal Code of the United States of Brazil, Decree No. 847, October 11, 1890, Article 402
look.prompt: Where does the law say capoeira is a crime? What does that tell you about where people played?

check.q: What did the Lei Áurea of 1888 do?
choices: It opened the first capoeira school.
check.why: The Golden Law, signed May 13, 1888, ended slavery in Brazil.

check.q: In what year did Brazil's Penal Code make capoeira a crime?
check.why: Article 402 of the Penal Code of October 1890 named capoeira as a crime.

check.why: The ban came two years after abolition and fell mostly on newly freed Black Brazilians.

lessons.title: Keeping the Art Alive
lessons.mainIdea: During the ban, people kept capoeira going in quieter places, especially in Salvador, Bahia.
reading: The ban lasted for decades. Police in Rio arrested many players in the 1890s. Some were sent to a prison island far off the coast. In Rio, the maltas broke apart. But capoeira did not disappear.

In Salvador, Bahia, people kept playing. Rodas met at dock areas, markets and street festivals. Many players were dockworkers and other working people. Older players taught younger ones by showing and singing. The songs carried history from one age to the next.

Many capoeira players had an *apelido*, or nickname. Mestres today often say nicknames helped hide real names from police. Historians say nicknames were also simply common in Brazil. Either way, the custom lasts. Many students still receive an apelido from their group.

words.d: a nickname given to a capoeira player by the group
a rule or law that forbids something

look.prompt: How many years passed between the Golden Law and the capoeira ban?

check.why: In Salvador, Bahia, people kept holding rodas at docks, markets and festivals.

check.q: What is an apelido?
check.why: An apelido is a nickname a capoeira player receives from the group.

check.q: How did older players pass capoeira to younger ones during the ban?
check.why: Capoeira was passed on person to person, and songs carried history across ages.

lessons.title: Mestre Bimba's Academy
lessons.mainIdea: Mestre Bimba opened a capoeira school in Salvador in 1932, and in 1937 it became the first capoeira school the state officially recognized.
reading: Manuel dos Reis Machado was born in Salvador in 1899 or 1900. People called him *Mestre* Bimba. Mestre means master teacher in Portuguese. He learned capoeira as a boy from an African-born teacher. As a young man, he worked as a dockworker and carpenter.

In 1932, Bimba opened a school in Salvador. It met indoors, with set class times. In 1937, the Bahia state government officially registered it. It was the first capoeira school to get that recognition. Bimba called his style Luta Regional Baiana, the regional fight of Bahia. Today it is called *Capoeira Regional*.

Bimba is known for strict school rules. Students were expected to be working or in school. He added a graduation ceremony. Many of his students were middle-class young men and university students. Bimba moved to Goiânia, in central Brazil, in 1973. He died there in 1974.

words.d: Portuguese for master; the title for a senior capoeira teacher
the style of capoeira started by Mestre Bimba in Salvador in the 1930s
a school where a skill or art is taught

look.title: Street Roda and Academy
look.text: Roda A meets on a festival day near the docks. Anyone may watch. The oldest players decide who plays. Roda B meets indoors on Tuesday evenings. It has a sign, a student list and a license from the state. One teacher leads it.
look.prompt: Which roda is more like Bimba's 1937 academy? What changed when capoeira moved indoors?

check.q: What does the title Mestre mean?
check.why: Mestre is Portuguese for master, the title for a senior capoeira teacher.

check.why: In 1937 the Bahia state government registered Bimba's school, the first capoeira school to be recognized.

check.q: What style of capoeira did Mestre Bimba start?

lessons.title: Mestre Pastinha and Angola
lessons.mainIdea: Mestre Pastinha founded a school in Salvador in 1941 to keep the older style called Capoeira Angola.
reading: Vicente Ferreira Pastinha was born in Salvador in 1889. He learned capoeira as a boy. He said his teacher was an African man named Benedito. People called him Mestre Pastinha. In 1941, he founded the Centro Esportivo de Capoeira Angola in Salvador.

*Capoeira Angola* is the name for the older style Pastinha worked to keep. The name honors Angola in Central Africa, where many ancestors came from. Pastinha's school kept a slower, older way of playing. Students wore matching yellow and black shirts, the colors of his favorite soccer club.

In 1964, Pastinha published a book titled Capoeira Angola. In 1966, his students traveled to the First World Festival of Negro Arts in Dakar, Senegal. There, capoeira was shown on a stage in Africa. Pastinha lost most of his sight in old age. He died in Salvador in 1981.

words.d: the older style of capoeira, kept and taught by Mestre Pastinha and others
a large public event that shows art, music or culture

look.title: Two Schools, One City
look.text: School 1: opened in Salvador in 1932, registered in 1937, led by Mestre Bimba, called Capoeira Regional. School 2: founded in Salvador in 1941, led by Mestre Pastinha, called Capoeira Angola. Both teachers learned as boys from African-born teachers.
look.prompt: What do the two schools share? What makes each one different?

check.q: What style did Mestre Pastinha work to keep?
check.why: Pastinha founded the Centro Esportivo de Capoeira Angola to keep the older Angola style.

check.q: Why is the style called Angola?
choices: It honors Angola in Central Africa, a homeland of many ancestors.

check.why: The name honors Angola, where many enslaved ancestors of Afro-Brazilians came from.

lessons.title: Cords and Batizados
lessons.mainIdea: Many capoeira groups mark progress with colored cords given at a ceremony called a batizado, but each group sets its own system.
reading: Mestre Bimba's school held graduations. Students received colored silk scarves. Later, many Regional groups switched to a *corda*, a colored cord tied at the waist. The cord shows how long a student has trained and what the group expects of them.

The ceremony where a new student gets a first cord is often called a *batizado*. The word means baptism in Portuguese. Many groups hold one each year. Guests and visiting mestres come. Many students also get their apelido at a batizado.

There is no one world body that sets capoeira ranks for everyone. Each group chooses its own colors and order. A green cord can mean one thing in one group and something else in another. Many Angola groups use no cords at all. There, respect comes from years in the roda.

words.d: a colored cord worn at the waist in many capoeira groups to show a student's level
Portuguese for baptism; a capoeira ceremony where students receive a first cord

look.title: Same Color, Two Groups
look.text: Two students meet at a festival. Both wear green cords. One student's group gives green to first-year students. The other student's group gives green only after about ten years. Neither group is wrong. There is no single capoeira ranking body.
look.prompt: Why can the same color mean different things? How could the students find out each other's level?

check.why: A batizado, Portuguese for baptism, is the ceremony where new students receive a first cord.

check.q: Who sets the order of cord colors in capoeira?

check.q: What did students at Mestre Bimba's school first receive at graduation?

lessons.title: Brazil Names a Treasure
lessons.mainIdea: In 2008, Brazil's national heritage office listed capoeira as part of the country's cultural heritage.
reading: Brazil's 1890 ban faded as schools opened in the 1930s. A new penal code came out in 1940. It no longer listed capoeira as a crime. More academies opened in Salvador, Rio and São Paulo in the following decades.

Brazil has a national office that protects heritage. It is called *IPHAN*, the National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage. In July 2008, IPHAN listed capoeira as part of Brazil's *cultural heritage*. It named two things: the roda itself and the craft of the mestres who teach it.

In 2010, Brazil passed a law called the Statute of Racial Equality. It aims to protect the rights of Black Brazilians. The law recognizes capoeira as a sport created in Brazil. It also supports teaching capoeira. The same country that once jailed players now protects the art.

words.d: Brazil's National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage, which protects buildings and traditions
the traditions, places and skills a people choose to protect and pass on

look.title: Two Government Papers
look.text: Paper 1, from 1890: capoeira in streets and squares is a crime, with two to six months in prison. Paper 2, from 2008: the roda and the craft of the mestres are part of Brazil's heritage. Both papers come from the government of Brazil.
look.prompt: What changed between the two papers? Who helped cause that change?

lessons.title: The World Honors the Circle
lessons.mainIdea: In 2014, UNESCO added the capoeira circle to its list of the world's living heritage, and capoeira schools now exist in many countries.
reading: *UNESCO* is a United Nations group for education, science and culture. It keeps a list of *intangible heritage*. Intangible means you cannot hold it in your hand. The list holds songs, dances, crafts and customs. In November 2014, UNESCO added the capoeira circle to that list.

UNESCO's record calls capoeira an Afro-Brazilian practice. It describes the roda as a place where people play, sing and learn together. It also notes the mestres who pass on the tradition. This was a major honor for an art Brazil had once banned.

Capoeira spread outside Brazil starting in the 1970s. Brazilian mestres opened schools in the United States and Europe. Today groups meet in dozens of countries, including in Chicago. Students around the world sing in Portuguese. Many travel to Salvador to learn from mestres there.

words.d: the United Nations group for education, science and culture
traditions you cannot hold, like songs, dances and customs, that people protect

chapters.title: Queensberry and the Ring
chapters.bigQuestion: Who decides the rules of boxing, and why do a gym, a commission and a school each answer differently?

story.title: Two Books on Two Desks
story.kicker: One book tells boxers how long a round lasts; the other tells a school which sports it runs.
paragraphs: A fifth-grade class in Chicago is building a history display. On the left desk sits a copy of the Queensberry Rules from 1867. The cover shows a pair of old leather gloves. Inside are twelve short rules for boxing matches.

On the right desk sits a thick handbook from the Illinois High School Association, the IHSA. The IHSA was founded in 1900. It runs state finals for Illinois high schools. Its list includes wrestling, track, basketball and many more sports.

One student reads the Queensberry page out loud. Rounds last three minutes. Rest lasts one minute. A boxer who is down has ten seconds to get up. Then another student searches the IHSA sports list. Boxing is not on it.

The class starts asking questions. If boxing has a rulebook, who uses it? Where do young boxers in Chicago train, if not on a school team? Their teacher writes three words on the board: gym, commission, school.

Each word names a different kind of group that shapes boxing. A gym is where people train. A commission is a state office that licenses professional fights. A school association decides which sports students play for their school. The class sets out to learn how each one began.
story.think: Why might a sport have a famous rulebook but still not be a school sport?

lessons.title: Boxers of Ancient Greece
lessons.mainIdea: Boxing is thousands of years old; the ancient Olympic Games added it in 688 BCE.
reading: On the Greek island of Santorini, called Thera in ancient times, lies the old town of Akrotiri. A volcano buried it more than 3,500 years ago. Archaeologists found a wall painting there. It shows two boys boxing, each with one glove. It is one of the oldest boxing pictures known.

The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia, in Greece. Greek records say boxing joined the Games in 688 BCE. Boxers wrapped their hands and wrists with long strips of leather. The Greek word for these wraps was *himantes*. There were no rounds and no weight classes.

Boxing was also popular in ancient Rome. Later, after the Roman Empire fell, it faded in Europe for centuries. When boxing returned in England in the 1700s, it grew from fairs and taverns. This is why historians call modern boxing an English sport with very old roots.

words.d: long leather strips ancient Greek boxers wrapped around their hands
a scientist who studies the past by digging up objects and places

look.title: A Wall Painting from Akrotiri
look.text: Picture a painted wall found under volcanic ash on the island of Thera. Two young boys face each other. Each wears a single glove on one hand. The painting is more than 3,500 years old. It was made long before any rulebook existed.
look.prompt: What does this painting tell you about how old boxing is? What can it not tell you?

check.why: Greek records say boxing joined the ancient Olympics in 688 BCE.

check.q: What were himantes?
choices: leather strips wrapped around the hands
check.why: Himantes were long leather wraps ancient Greek boxers wore on their hands and wrists.

check.q: Where was the ancient painting of two boys boxing found?
check.why: The painting was found in Akrotiri, on the island of Thera, buried by a volcano.

lessons.title: Broughton Writes Rules
lessons.mainIdea: In 1743, the London boxer Jack Broughton wrote the first set of boxing rules in England.
reading: Jack Broughton was a champion boxer in London in the 1700s. In 1743, he opened his own boxing hall, called an amphitheatre. Crowds paid to watch. Around this time, a fighter died after a bout with Broughton. Broughton wanted fights to have clear rules.

In August 1743, he posted a short list of rules at his amphitheatre. They are known as *Broughton's Rules*. They set up a chalked square in the middle of the stage. They said who could be on the stage. They set how long a fallen boxer had to return. Umpires settled arguments.

Broughton's fights were fought with bare fists. But he is often credited with using padded *mufflers* for practice. Mufflers were early boxing gloves. They were only for training, not for prize fights. Gloves would not be required in matches for over a hundred years.

words.d: the first written boxing rules in England, posted by Jack Broughton in London in 1743
padded practice gloves of the 1700s, an early form of boxing gloves
a hall with seats around a central space for watching events

look.title: Why Write It Down?
look.text: Before 1743, each fight's rules were argued out on the day. Fans, fighters and backers often disagreed. After a fighter died, Jack Broughton posted rules on the wall of his London hall. Anyone who fought there had to follow them.
look.prompt: How does a written list on a wall change a sport? Who gains power when rules are written?

check.q: Who wrote the first set of boxing rules in England?
check.why: Jack Broughton posted his rules at his London amphitheatre in 1743.

check.q: What were mufflers?
check.why: Mufflers were padded gloves for practice, an early form of boxing gloves.

check.q: Were Broughton's prize fights fought with gloves?
choices: No, they were fought with bare fists.
check.why: Broughton's prize fights were bare-fisted; mufflers were only for training.

lessons.title: The London Prize Ring
lessons.mainIdea: The London Prize Ring Rules of 1838 governed bare-knuckle prize fights, which were often against the law.
reading: In 1838, a new set of rules replaced Broughton's. They were called the *London Prize Ring Rules*. They were revised in 1853. A prize ring was a fight for a money prize. These rules called for a square of ropes and stakes, 24 feet on each side.

Under these rules, boxers fought with bare knuckles. A round ended when a boxer went down. A fight had no set number of rounds. Some fights lasted for hours. Injuries were common, and some fighters died.

Prize fighting was against the law in much of Britain and the United States. Organizers often hid the location until the last minute. Fans sometimes rode special trains to a secret field. Police might arrive and stop the fight. Then the crowd would move somewhere else.

words.d: the rules for bare-knuckle prize fights written in 1838 and revised in 1853
a boxing match fought for money
boxing without gloves

look.title: A Ring That Is a Square
look.text: Long ago, a boxing ring was simply a circle of watchers standing around two fighters. Then rules called for ropes and stakes. By 1838, the London Prize Ring Rules described a roped square, 24 feet on a side. People kept calling it a ring.
look.prompt: Why do you think the old word ring stayed, even after the shape became a square?

check.q: What is a prize fight?
check.why: A prize fight is a match fought for a money prize, as under the London Prize Ring Rules.

check.q: Under the London Prize Ring Rules, when did a round end?
choices: when the bell rang at noon
check.why: Under the 1838 rules, a round ended when a boxer went down, so rounds had no set length.

check.q: Why did organizers often hide where a prize fight would happen?
choices: Prize fighting was often against the law.
check.why: Prize fighting was illegal in many places, so locations were hidden from police.

lessons.title: Chambers Writes, Queensberry Signs
lessons.mainIdea: John Graham Chambers wrote the Queensberry Rules, published in 1867 and named for the Marquess of Queensberry, who backed them.
reading: John Graham Chambers was a Welsh sportsman and writer. In 1866, he helped found the Amateur Athletic Club in London. An *amateur* is someone who competes without being paid. Chambers wanted boxing for amateurs that was safer and more orderly.

Chambers wrote a new set of twelve rules. They were published in 1867. A Scottish nobleman, John Sholto Douglas, the Marquess of Queensberry, supported them. A marquess is a high noble title in Britain. His name went on the rules. They became known as the *Queensberry Rules*.

The first rule called for a fair stand-up boxing match in a 24-foot ring. Another rule banned wrestling and hugging. Amateur clubs used the rules first. In England, the Amateur Boxing Association formed in 1880. Professional boxers adopted the Queensberry Rules more slowly, over the next 25 years.

words.d: twelve boxing rules written by John Graham Chambers and published in 1867, requiring gloves and timed rounds
someone who competes without being paid
a high noble title in Britain

look.title: Rule One
look.text: To be a fair stand-up boxing match in a 24-foot ring, or as near that size as practicable.
look.cite: The Queensberry Rules, rule 1, drawn up by John Graham Chambers, published 1867
look.prompt: What does rule one set up before any boxing starts? Why might the ring's size matter?

check.q: Who actually wrote the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: John Graham Chambers wrote the rules; the Marquess of Queensberry supported them and lent his name.

check.q: What is an amateur?
choices: a person who competes without being paid
check.why: An amateur competes without pay; Chambers wrote the rules first for amateur clubs.

check.q: In what year were the Queensberry Rules published?
check.why: The Queensberry Rules were published in 1867.

lessons.title: Gloves, Rounds, Ten Seconds
lessons.mainIdea: The Queensberry Rules required gloves, three-minute rounds with a one-minute rest, and ten seconds for a fallen boxer to rise.
reading: The Queensberry Rules changed three big things. First, boxers had to wear gloves. The rules called for fair-sized gloves of the best quality. Under the old prize ring rules, fists were bare. Gloves made boxing look more like a sport for gentlemen's clubs.

Second, each *round* lasted three minutes. A round is one timed part of a match. Between rounds came one minute of rest. Before this, rounds had no set length. The clock made matches easier to judge and to follow.

Third, a boxer who went down had ten seconds to get up without help. If not, the other boxer won. This became the famous ten *count*. A referee judged the match. These rules are still the base of boxing rules today, more than 150 years later.

words.d: one timed part of a boxing match
the seconds a referee counts aloud while a fallen boxer tries to get up
the official who controls a match and enforces the rules

look.title: Timing in the Queensberry Rules
rows: Time to rise after a fall
look.cite: The Queensberry Rules, published 1867, rules 3 and 4
look.prompt: How many seconds long is one round plus one rest?

check.q: How long was a round under the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: The Queensberry Rules set rounds at three minutes, with one minute of rest.

check.q: What is a round?
choices: one timed part of a match
check.why: A round is one timed part of a boxing match.

check.q: How did the Queensberry Rules differ from the London Prize Ring Rules?
choices: They ended rounds only when a boxer fell.
They required gloves and timed rounds.
check.why: Queensberry required gloves and three-minute rounds; the prize ring used bare fists and untimed rounds.

lessons.title: The Last Bare-Knuckle Title
lessons.mainIdea: In 1892, the heavyweight championship was first won under Queensberry Rules with gloves, ending the bare-knuckle title era.
reading: John L. Sullivan was born in Boston in 1858. He became the most famous boxer in America. In 1889, he fought Jake Kilrain in Richburg, Mississippi. It was a bare-knuckle fight under London Prize Ring Rules. It lasted 75 rounds. Sullivan won. It was the last bare-knuckle heavyweight title fight.

On September 7, 1892, Sullivan fought James J. Corbett in New Orleans, Louisiana. This time both men wore gloves. The fight used the Queensberry Rules. Corbett won in the 21st round. He became the first heavyweight champion under the Queensberry Rules.

After 1892, professional boxing in America moved to gloves and timed rounds. Bare-knuckle fights faded away. Boxing began to move into lit indoor halls with sold tickets. Newspapers covered big fights, and telegraph wires carried the results across the country.

words.d: the class for the heaviest boxers; its champion was the best known
the name of champion in a sport, held until someone wins it away

look.title: From Bare Fists to Gloves
look.cite: Broughton's Rules, 1743; London Prize Ring Rules, 1838; Queensberry Rules, 1867; heavyweight title records
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Queensberry Rules and the first Queensberry heavyweight title?

check.q: Who won the 1892 fight in New Orleans?
check.why: James J. Corbett beat Sullivan in 1892, the first heavyweight title fight under the Queensberry Rules.

check.q: What was special about the 1889 Sullivan–Kilrain fight?
choices: It was the last bare-knuckle heavyweight title fight.
It was the first Olympic boxing match.
check.why: Sullivan beat Kilrain in Mississippi in 1889 in the last bare-knuckle heavyweight title fight.

check.q: How did professional boxing change after 1892?
choices: It moved to gloves and timed rounds.
check.why: After Corbett's win under the Queensberry Rules, pro boxing used gloves and timed rounds.

lessons.title: Breaking the Color Line
lessons.mainIdea: Jack Johnson became the first Black world heavyweight champion in 1908, after years when white champions refused to fight Black boxers.
reading: In the late 1800s, many white champions drew a *color line*. That meant they refused to fight Black boxers. John L. Sullivan would not fight the Black boxer Peter Jackson, who had won the Australian heavyweight title. The color line kept the heavyweight title for white boxers only.

Jack Johnson was born in Galveston, Texas, in 1878. His parents had been enslaved. On December 26, 1908, in Sydney, Australia, he beat Tommy Burns. Johnson became the first Black world heavyweight champion. In 1910, he beat James Jeffries in Reno, Nevada. White mobs then attacked Black Americans in many cities.

Johnson lived in Chicago and opened a club there in 1912. In 1913, he was convicted under an unfair use of a federal law. He left the country and lost his title in 1915. In 2018, President Donald Trump gave him a *pardon*, long after his death in 1946.

words.d: a rule, written or unwritten, that kept Black athletes out of contests with white athletes
an official act that forgives a person convicted of a crime

look.title: A Title and a Line
look.text: In 1892, the heavyweight title belonged to whoever beat the champion. But champions chose whom to fight. Some champions refused to fight any Black challenger. In 1908, Jack Johnson finally got a title match, in Australia, and won.
look.prompt: How could a sport have written rules and still be unfair? What does the color line show?

check.q: What was the color line in boxing?
choices: a painted line on the floor
the refusal of white champions to fight Black boxers
check.why: The color line was the practice of white champions refusing to fight Black boxers.

check.q: Who became the first Black world heavyweight champion in 1908?
check.why: Jack Johnson beat Tommy Burns in Sydney, Australia, on December 26, 1908.

check.q: What is a pardon?
choices: an official act that forgives a conviction
check.why: A pardon forgives a conviction; Jack Johnson received one in 2018, long after his death.

lessons.title: Women Enter the Ring
lessons.mainIdea: Women were kept out of official amateur boxing in the United States until a 1993 court case, and women's boxing joined the Olympics in 2012.
reading: Women boxed in public as far back as the 1700s in London. But for most of history, boxing groups kept women out. In the United States, USA Boxing, the body for amateur boxing, did not allow women to compete. Many states also would not license women as professional boxers.

In 1993, Dallas Malloy, a 16-year-old from Washington State, took USA Boxing to court. A judge ruled that she should be allowed to box. That October, she fought in the first amateur women's bout USA Boxing approved. USA Boxing soon opened its events to women across the country.

Boxing had been an *Olympic* sport for men since 1904 in St. Louis. Women had to wait until the London Games in 2012. That year, Claressa Shields of Flint, Michigan, won gold in the middleweight class. She was 17. She won Olympic gold again in 2016.

words.d: part of the Olympic Games, the world sports festival held every four years
the national body that runs amateur boxing in the United States

look.title: Women's Olympic Weight Classes
look.cite: International Olympic Committee, official results of the 2012, 2020 and 2024 Games
look.prompt: How many more women's weight classes were there in 2024 than in 2012?

check.q: Who took USA Boxing to court in 1993 for the right to box?
check.why: Sixteen-year-old Dallas Malloy sued USA Boxing in 1993 and won the right to box.

check.q: When did women's boxing first appear at the Olympic Games?
check.why: Women's boxing first appeared at the London Olympics in 2012.

check.q: What does the chart show about women's Olympic boxing?
choices: The number of weight classes grew from 3 to 6.
The number of weight classes shrank.
It has only one weight class.
check.why: Women's weight classes went from 3 in 2012 to 5 in 2020 and 6 in 2024.

lessons.title: Not on the School List
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA, founded in 1900, runs state finals in many sports, but boxing is not one of them, and college boxing ended after a death in 1960.
reading: The *IHSA* is the Illinois High School Association. It was founded in 1900. It decides which sports Illinois high schools play for state titles. Boys wrestling crowned its first state champions in 1937. Girls wrestling held its first state finals in 2022. Boxing is not on the IHSA list.

Colleges once had boxing teams. The NCAA, the main college sports body, held boxing championships from 1932 to 1960. In April 1960, a University of Wisconsin boxer named Charlie Mohr collapsed after a bout at the NCAA tournament. He died days later. Wisconsin dropped boxing, and the NCAA ended its championship.

Schools choose sports with care for student safety. Doctors' groups have raised concerns about head injuries in boxing. So in American schools, boxing mostly stayed off the team list. Young boxers found other places to train. Those places are gyms, clubs and community centers.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, founded in 1900, which runs high school state finals
the National Collegiate Athletic Association, the main body for college sports in the United States

look.title: Two Handbooks
look.text: Handbook A, 1867: twelve rules for boxing with gloves, three-minute rounds and a ten count. Handbook B, from the IHSA: rules for Illinois school state finals, including wrestling since 1937, with no boxing listed. Both are rule books. They answer different questions.
look.prompt: What question does each handbook answer? Why can both be right at once?

check.q: When was the IHSA founded?
check.why: The Illinois High School Association was founded in 1900.

check.q: Why did the NCAA end its boxing championship after 1960?
choices: A college boxer, Charlie Mohr, died after a tournament bout.
check.why: Charlie Mohr of Wisconsin died after a bout at the 1960 NCAA tournament, and college boxing ended.

check.q: Which of these has an IHSA state final?
check.why: IHSA boys wrestling began state finals in 1937; boxing is not on the IHSA list.

lessons.title: The Town Gym
lessons.mainIdea: Community gyms, church leagues and newspaper tournaments became the places where young Americans learned to box.
reading: In 1930, Bishop Bernard Sheil started the Catholic Youth Organization, or CYO, in Chicago. Boxing was one of its biggest programs. CYO tournaments filled the Chicago Stadium with fans. Boys of many faiths and backgrounds took part. The CYO gave city kids coaches, gyms and a place to belong.

Newspapers ran tournaments too. In the 1920s, the Chicago Tribune began running *Golden Gloves* tournaments for amateur boxers. Other cities started their own. Winners from different cities met in big matches. Golden Gloves events still run across the United States today.

In 1954, a 12-year-old in Louisville, Kentucky, had his bicycle stolen. He told a police officer named Joe Martin, who coached boxing at the Columbia Gym. The boy was Cassius Clay. He later won Olympic gold in 1960 and took the name Muhammad Ali. His path started in a town gym.

words.d: amateur boxing tournaments first run by newspapers in the 1920s, including the Chicago Tribune
a gym run by a town, church or club, open to local people

look.title: Three Doors to the Ring
look.text: Door 1: a church youth program in Chicago, starting in 1930. Door 2: a newspaper tournament with a golden glove as its symbol. Door 3: a police officer's boxing class in a Louisville gym. None of these is a school team.
look.prompt: Who ran each door? Why might these groups offer boxing when schools did not?

check.why: Bishop Bernard Sheil founded the CYO in Chicago in 1930, with boxing as a big program.

check.q: Which newspaper began Golden Gloves tournaments in the 1920s?
check.why: The Chicago Tribune began running Golden Gloves tournaments in the 1920s.

check.q: How did Cassius Clay, later Muhammad Ali, start boxing?
choices: at a gym where police officer Joe Martin coached
check.why: After his bike was stolen in 1954, Clay met officer Joe Martin, who coached at Louisville's Columbia Gym.

lessons.title: Commissions and Crowds
lessons.mainIdea: States created athletic commissions to license and oversee professional boxing, such as New York's commission in 1920.
reading: For years, professional boxing was banned or barely allowed in many states. In 1920, New York passed the Walker Law. It made pro boxing legal in the state. It also created the New York State Athletic Commission. An athletic *commission* is a state office that oversees professional fights.

A commission gives licenses to boxers, referees and promoters. A *license* is official permission to do a job. Commissions require medical checks. They can stop a boxer from fighting. Other states set up their own commissions in the years that followed.

Big fights drew huge crowds. On September 22, 1927, Gene Tunney fought Jack Dempsey at Soldier Field in Chicago. More than 100,000 people came. It is remembered as the Long Count fight. A new rule sent a boxer to a neutral corner before the referee began counting, and that delay became famous.

words.d: a state office that licenses and oversees professional fights
official permission to do a job or activity
a person or company that sets up and sells tickets to fights

look.title: Three Groups, Three Jobs
look.text: The gym: where a boxer trains, run by a club, church or owner. The commission: a state office that licenses professional fighters and checks their health. The school association: decides which sports students play for their school. Each group has its own rules.

check.why: A license is official permission; commissions license boxers, referees and promoters.

check.q: Where was the 1927 Long Count fight held?

review.why: John Graham Chambers wrote them; the Marquess of Queensberry lent his name.

review.q: Which set of rules came first?
